For adults in [City] who want to strengthen their reading and writing skills, these everyday tasks can take extra time or require help from someone they trust. According to [state adult literacy survey, year], [X%] of adults in [reported geography] score at [defined proficiency level], compared with [Y%] in [comparable geography or prior survey year]. In [City], [local employer, school, or agency] recently [documented change that increased reading or writing demands], making literacy support especially timely for residents navigating that change. **The gap is access to instruction that helps adults build reading and writing skills while practicing the tasks they face today.**

The need is especially pressing for [priority population] in [City], including residents of [ZIP or neighborhood]. The U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey ([year] five-year estimates, tables [IDs]) reports that [X%] of adults age 25 and older in [geography] lack a high school credential, and [Y%] of [relevant population] face [documented barrier, such as limited household internet access or lack of a vehicle]. These figures do not measure literacy proficiency; they help explain the conditions that can make instruction harder to reach. For residents who [locally documented scheduling, transportation, or technology constraint], an available class is not necessarily one they can attend consistently. **The gap is literacy instruction that residents in [priority area] can reach and attend regularly through [actual program location, schedule, or delivery option].**

Literacy goals also emerge at moments when families and adult learners are making decisions about education. In [year], [local school district or community college enrollment report] recorded [verified figure on family literacy referrals, adult education enrollment, or another relevant indicator]. As one participant explained, “[Insert a verified quote about a specific barrier to attending or returning to class.]” This distinction matters for [Organization]: recruiting more learners will not improve access if the same barriers prevent them from returning after the first session. **The gap is a way for learners to keep making progress when [documented barrier] interrupts attendance, through [actual retention or reentry support].**

## Program Design & Activities

Adults in [City] need literacy instruction they can start promptly, attend consistently, and use before the next job application or school deadline. [Organization] will pair level-matched reading and writing instruction with practice on everyday tasks and a clear route back after an absence, addressing both the skills learners want to build and the barriers that keep them from class.

### Core Activity 1: Small-group reading and writing instruction

A [qualified adult literacy instructor] will lead groups of up to [number] adults at [accessible site in ZIP]. Each group will meet [number] times per week for [minutes] per session over a [number]-week cycle. Using intake results, the instructor will group learners by instructional level and teach the skills each group needs, such as decoding unfamiliar words, reading for meaning, or writing a clear response. Sessions will move from instructor modeling to guided practice and then independent work, with brief skill checks to guide the next lesson. [Organization] will offer classes at [days and times], selected to address [documented scheduling or access barrier] in [ZIP]. This adds seats at the instructional levels and times that [referral records or service inventory, year] identify as hardest to access.

### Core Activity 2: Applied literacy practice

At [site in City], the instructor and [trained tutor or program staff role] will lead a [minutes]-minute practice lab [frequency], scheduled [alongside regular classes or at a separate accessible time]. Learners will choose tasks tied to their goals, such as interpreting a school notice, following enrollment instructions, or drafting a response on a job application. Staff will model how to identify key information, break instructions into steps, and check a written response. Learners will then try a comparable task independently, using sample or redacted materials. Staff will record which steps each learner can complete without prompting and use that information to plan further practice. The lab responds to feedback from [City] residents who want to handle these tasks independently: learners can work toward a deadline while building skills they can carry into the next task.

### Core Activity 3: Attendance and reentry support

A [learner support role] based at [site in ZIP] will review attendance weekly and hold a [minutes]-minute check-in with each learner at [frequency], in person or by [approved contact method]. At enrollment, staff and learners will identify likely attendance barriers and agree on how and when staff should reach out. After [number] missed sessions, staff will contact the learner within [number] business days to identify what would make returning possible. Depending on the barrier and available options, staff will arrange [makeup session or alternate class time], connect the learner to [partner support], or reserve a place in the next cycle. Learners who return will resume at an appropriate point rather than repeat intake. This gives adults in [ZIP] a way to keep one missed class from becoming a lost cycle.

### Participant pathway and checkpoints

**Intake → placement → services → follow-up.** At intake, staff confirm eligibility, document a learner-selected goal and access needs, and collect a baseline reading or writing measure. The instructor uses the results to recommend a class and confirms placement after [number] sessions. During the cycle, staff review attendance weekly and check progress at midpoint, adjusting instruction or supports as needed. At exit, the instructor repeats the baseline measure using [tool and scoring method], reviews progress toward the learner’s goal, and agrees on a next step. At [number] days after exit, staff check whether the learner has used the skill or connected with a next-step service. Learners who pause can reenter through the same contact rather than start over.

### Evidence base

The design draws on adult literacy research on assessment-informed, explicit instruction with guided practice [adult literacy evidence review, year]. Applied tasks and individualized follow-up draw on [evidence source on contextualized instruction or adult learner persistence, year].

### Feasibility and rollout

A [program lead, FTE] will oversee delivery and partner coordination; [number] instructors totaling [FTE] will staff [number] groups per cycle; and a [learner support role, FTE] will manage intake, attendance outreach, and follow-up. With [number] seats per group and [number] cycles per year, the enrollment target is [number] unique adults, accounting for learners who continue across cycles. [Referral partner] will refer eligible adults, and [site partner] will provide [space and hours]. **Quarter 1:** confirm partner roles and site access, train staff, and begin intake. **Quarter 2:** deliver the first cycle and review attendance and midpoint skill data. **Quarter 3:** run subsequent cycles and adjust schedules or placement based on participation and demand. **Quarter 4:** complete final assessments and follow-up, review results with partners, and set the next enrollment schedule.

### Phrasing hooks

- “The intake assessment guides placement; it does not determine whether a learner deserves a seat.”
- “Learners practice on tasks they need to complete now and build skills they can use again.”
- “A missed class triggers outreach and a plan to return—not a new application.”
- “We are adding seats at the times and instructional levels that local referral records show are hardest to access.”

### Quick logic model: one-page figure

- **Inputs →** Grant funds, program lead, literacy instructors, learner support staff, accessible space in [ZIP], assessment tools, and referral partners.
- **Activity 1 →** Deliver level-matched small-group reading and writing instruction using explicit teaching, guided practice, and skill checks.
- **Activity 2 →** Run applied practice labs focused on learner-selected work, school, and everyday tasks.
- **Activity 3 →** Monitor attendance, contact learners after missed sessions, and arrange retention or reentry supports.
- **Outputs →** [number] unique adults enrolled; [number] instructional sessions and labs delivered; [number] learners receiving attendance or reentry support.
- **Short-term outcomes →** By cycle end, [percentage] of learners with paired assessments improve on [skill measure], and [percentage] of assessed learners complete a comparable literacy task with fewer prompts.
- **Long-term outcomes →** At [follow-up interval], [percentage] of respondents report using a practiced skill independently, and [percentage] report completing their identified next step in education, employment, or daily life.

## Outcomes & Evaluation

[Organization] will measure whether adults in [City], including residents of [ZIP], build reading and writing skills, use those skills independently, and stay connected to instruction when attendance is interrupted. Enrollment tells us whether we are reaching learners; assessments, attendance records, and follow-up tell us whether the program is helping them make progress. We will review results during each cycle so staff can address barriers while learners still have time to benefit.

### SMART outcomes

1. **Reading and writing skill gains.** By the end of each instructional cycle, at least [target percentage] of learners with both intake and exit assessments will improve by at least [meaningful gain threshold] on their designated reading or writing measure, as scored using [tool name]. Each learner’s baseline is their intake score of [intake score]; the program benchmark is [baseline percentage] of learners meeting the same gain threshold in [year], if comparable records exist.
2. **Independent completion of practical tasks.** By cycle end, at least [target percentage] of learners with paired task assessments will complete [number] of [total number] essential steps without prompting on a task comparable to the one they attempted at intake. Staff will score both tasks using [tool name]. The baseline is [baseline percentage] of the same learners meeting that standard at intake.
3. **Reentry after an interruption.** By the end of the grant year, at least [target percentage] of learners who reach the outreach threshold of [number] missed sessions and have [number] days available for follow-up will attend a class or makeup session within that period. The baseline is [baseline percentage] of learners who returned within the same period after meeting the same threshold in [year].
4. **Use of literacy skills beyond class.** At [number] days after exit, at least [target percentage] of follow-up respondents will report using a practiced skill independently for a specific work, school, or everyday task during the previous [number] days. The baseline is [baseline percentage] of those same respondents reporting independent use of the selected skill over an equivalent period at intake. We will report the follow-up response rate alongside the result.

### Evaluation design and data collection

[Organization] will use a pre/post design to track change within learners, with attendance records and follow-up interviews to assess reentry and skill use. This design will show what changed for learners with paired data; it will not establish that the program alone caused the change. Where comparable historical data are unavailable, we will identify the first eligible grant cohort as the baseline for future comparisons and label it separately from the grant target.

| Checkpoint | What we will collect | Who will collect it |
|---|---|---|
| **Intake** | Baseline skill score and practical-task rubric; learner-selected goal, recent skill use, and access barriers | Intake staff record goals and barriers; instructors administer and score [tool name]. |
| **Midpoint** | Brief skill check, progress toward the learner’s goal, attendance, and any support or placement changes | Instructors record skill checks; learner support staff review attendance and document outreach. |
| **Exit** | Comparable skill assessment and practical task, scored using the same criteria as at intake; next-step plan | Instructors administer and score assessments; learner support staff record the next step. |
| **Follow-up** | Recent independent skill use, a concrete example, and progress toward the next step | Learner support staff conduct a brief survey or interview using [tool name] and log contact attempts and responses. |

The [evaluation lead] will check records for missing scores, duplicate enrollments, and inconsistent scoring, then calculate results by cycle and across the grant year. Reports will show how many learners enrolled, how many had paired measures, and how many responded to follow-up. Missing assessments will be reported separately—not counted as either gains or no gains.

### Privacy and continuous improvement

[Organization] will explain what data are collected, how they are used, and which follow-up questions are optional. Staff will use participant IDs in analysis files, keep names and contact details separate in a restricted system, and limit access by role. Funder reports will use aggregate results and suppress small groups where disclosure could identify a learner. Records will be retained and securely deleted under [retention policy].

The program lead, instructors, and learner support staff will review attendance and outreach monthly and examine skill gains and assessment completion after each cycle. If a class time shows repeated absences, the program lead will test a scheduling change; if learners repeatedly struggle with a task step, instructors will revise the lesson and check the next cycle’s results. The program lead will assign each change an owner and review date.

### Example dashboard indicators

| Indicator | Calculation | Reporting cadence |
|---|---|---|
| **Output: Unique adults served** | Count of distinct participant IDs with at least one attended class or practice lab during the reporting period. Deduplicate across cycles for the year-to-date total. | Monthly and quarterly |
| **Outcome: Meaningful skill gain** | Learners who meet the gain threshold ÷ learners with valid paired intake and exit scores × 100. Show the numerator, denominator, and paired-assessment coverage. | At cycle close and quarterly |

**Baseline sources to pull**
- **Local intake records:** [Organization], [year], de-identified intake scores and practical-task ratings from [tool name].
- **Local program records:** [Organization] or [partner], [year], attendance and reentry logs; confirm that absence thresholds and return windows are comparable.
- **State adult literacy survey:** [state agency], [year], [reported geography and proficiency definition]. Use as context, not as a substitute for a participant baseline.

**Phrasing hooks**
- “Enrollment measures reach; paired assessments measure progress.”
- “Learners show what they can do without prompting, not just what they practiced in class.”
- “We review results while there is still time to improve the current cycle.”

---

## Budget Narrative

[Organization] requests **$[request amount]** toward a total program cost of **$[total program cost]** for [grant period]. The budget supports literacy instruction, applied practice, and attendance and reentry support for [number] unique adults in [City], with priority outreach in [ZIP]. Costs are based on [year] salary rates, [vendor quotes or current price estimates], and the staffing and service schedule described in the Program Design section.

**Personnel and fringe — $[amount].** The program lead ([FTE]) will oversee delivery, staff supervision, and partner coordination. Literacy instructors ([combined FTE or total hours]) will teach [number] groups per cycle, prepare lessons, run practice labs, and score assessments. The learner support role ([FTE or total hours]) will handle intake, attendance outreach, reentry, and follow-up. Personnel costs reflect [annual salary × grant-funded FTE × share of year, or hourly rate × hours]. Fringe is calculated at [rate]% of eligible wages under [Organization]’s benefits policy.

**Instruction, access, and evaluation — $[amount].** Instructional materials and assessment costs cover [number] learner sets at $[unit cost] and [number] licenses or scoring fees for [tool name] at $[unit cost]. Where permitted by the funder, [access support] will address [documented barrier] at $[unit cost] per [unit], up to [number] units. Evaluation costs cover [data system, scoring, or analysis expense not already included in personnel], allowing staff to track learner progress without charging the same work twice.

**Space, partner contributions, and indirect costs — $[amount requested].** [Site partner] will provide [space or hours] at [documented rate or no charge]. Confirmed in-kind support of $[amount], valued using [basis], will be shown separately from grant-funded expenses and counted as match only if eligible. Indirect costs of $[amount] apply the funder-permitted rate of [rate]% to [approved cost base]. The budget table distinguishes the grant request, other cash support, and any eligible in-kind contributions.

**Cost effectiveness.** At planned enrollment, the grant request equals **$[amount] per participant** ($[request amount] ÷ [number] unique adults), and the total program cost equals **$[amount] per participant** ($[total program cost] ÷ [number] unique adults). Each learner is counted once, even if they attend more than one cycle. Small-group instruction makes it possible to serve multiple learners at the same instructional level, while individual support is targeted to placement, missed sessions, and reentry. At year-end, [Organization] will compare actual spending with the number of unique adults served and the number who meet the defined skill-gain threshold, noting assessment coverage when reporting cost per measured gain.
